2026-11-01|ls-assigned-land: Assigned land: why it cannot be sold and what the law says Land School · source: “Assigned Land in India: Why It Cannot Be Sold and What the Law Says” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Assigned land = government surplus/wasteland granted to landless poor families for cultivation or house sites — possession and use, NOT free ownership. Transfers are prohibited or void under state land-reform laws; a registered sale deed changes nothing. The government can RESUME the land at any time, with no compensation to the buyer — and buying it can carry up to six months’ jail. Narrow exceptions: inheritance by heirs, bank mortgages, and good-faith pre-Act purchases by landless poor persons. The whole defence is two checks: the revenue record’s remarks and the Section 22-A prohibited list. What assigned land is Government surplus or wasteland handed to landless poor persons — typically agricultural labourers or SC/ST families — for cultivation or as a house site, under land-reform and welfare schemes. What transfers is possession and limited use rights; ownership stays CONDITIONAL with the state. The condition that matters to every buyer: the grant usually prohibits sale. Why the law bans its sale The point of assignment is welfare — land in the hands of the landless. If assignees could sell, the poor would be bought out for quick cash and the policy would defeat itself; so state laws (in Telangana, the Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act) bar selling, gifting, leasing or otherwise transferring without government permission, and declare violating transfers invalid. What “void ab initio” means Treated as if the transaction never legally happened — no title passes, ever. Even land that changed hands TEN times through ten registered deeds: every link is equally invalid. A registered document does not make you the owner here; the paper has no legal weight at all. One narrow protection exists: a landless poor person who bought in good faith, for value, from the original assignee BEFORE the Act commenced and was in possession on that date — it protects the poor, not an investor. Definition — Void ab initio: void “from the beginning” — not cancelled later, but never valid at any moment. Nothing downstream of it can be valid either. What happens if it is sold anyway The government can resume the land at ANY time — no limitation period runs in its favour going away — and reassign it to another eligible landless family. The buyer gets no compensation; no civil court can decree the sale into existence. And the consequence sellers never mention: acquiring assigned land in breach of the prohibition is an OFFENCE carrying up to six months’ imprisonment. The buyer is not just a victim in this law’s eyes. Transferability by land category Category Freely transferable? Notes Patta (private) land Yes Ordinary sale deed + registration Assigned land No Transfer void; resumption + penal risk Tribal-area land Highly restricted Transfers to non-tribals barred in scheduled areas Ceiling-surplus land No Vested in government for redistribution Endowment (temple) land No Alienation needs statutory sanction, rarely given Forest land No Central law bars de-reservation without approval What an assignee CAN do Cultivate for the family; pass the land to legal heirs (inheritance is generally not a prohibited transfer); mortgage it to a scheduled bank, co-operative or notified institution — the one security the Act permits; build a house where the assignment was a house site. And in some states, apply to the Collector for DE-RESTRICTION — converting it into regular patta land eligible for sale once eligibility conditions are met. Rules vary; the revenue authority’s word is the only one that counts. How to check whether a plot is assigned Pull the latest Record of Rights from the state revenue department and read the REMARKS column for “assigned”, “granted” or restriction notes. Check the state’s prohibited-property register (Section 22-A list) for the survey number. Ask the local revenue office directly. And read the original ASSIGNMENT ORDER — it states plainly whether transfer is prohibited. Fifteen minutes of record-reading is the difference between owning land and owning a legal dead end. Example: The classic Hyderabad-belt trap: a corridor plot at 40% below market, seller waving a registered deed from a 2009 purchase. The RoR remarks column reads “asgd”. That deed — and the one before it — are both void; the discount was the disclosure. Walk away; no lawyer can cure it. If you are the assignee wanting to sell Apply to the competent revenue authority for removal of the transfer restriction where state law permits, BEFORE entering any agreement. For SC/ST or tribal-origin land, confirm whether Collector approval is mandatory. Selling first and regularising later is not a sequence the law recognises. Quick answers (FAQ) Can assigned land be sold after N years? No automatic ripening — only formal de-restriction changes its status. Why do registered deeds exist on assigned land? Because registration only blocks parcels actually on the prohibited list; the registrar’s stamp never validates a void transfer. Can family inherit it? Yes — heirs succeed; that is not a prohibited transfer. Can it be mortgaged? Only to banks/institutions the Act permits. Can it ever become freehold? In some states, via Collector-approved conversion to patta land. Bottom line Assigned land is the one category where late homework has NO remedy — no cure, no compensation, no sympathetic court. The RoR remarks and the 22-A list, checked before any money moves, are the entire safeguard. For you: For a plotting developer this is the first gate on every parcel — before price, before layout dreams: Dharani/RoR remarks + 22-A check on each survey number. One assigned survey number inside an assembled venture can poison the whole layout’s marketability. Make the check a fixed line item in your acquisition template. The rural test is mechanical: the nearest municipality’s census population, and aerial distance of 2 / 6 / 8 km. Urban agricultural land is taxed like any property; long-term starts at 24 months. Section 54B exemption needs TWO years of actual farming before sale, reinvestment in farmland within two years, and a three-year lock-in on the new land. Section 50C lets the taxman substitute the stamp-duty value when you sell below it. When the tax applies at all One question decides everything: is the land RURAL or URBAN under the Income Tax Act? Rural agricultural land is excluded from the very definition of a capital asset by Section 2(14)(iii) — no capital asset, no capital gain, nothing to tax. Urban agricultural land gets no carve-out and is taxed like any other asset. Two owners can sell what looks like the same plot and one pays nothing while the other owes tax on the whole gain — purely because of where the land sits. The rural test — mechanical, not agricultural Nothing to do with how the land is farmed; everything to do with location and population. Land is RURAL if it lies outside a municipality or cantonment of 10,000+ people, AND outside these aerial distances from those limits: 2 km where the population is 10,000–1 lakh; 6 km where it is 1–10 lakh; 8 km where it exceeds 10 lakh. Population comes from the last published census; distance is measured AERIALLY — as the crow flies, not as the road winds. Inside the limits = urban agricultural land = taxable. One nuance: the exemption attaches to the LAND — a farmhouse, well or standing trees sold in the same deal are valued and treated separately. Example: Two farmers sell near Hyderabad (population >10 lakh, so the 8 km band applies). One’s land sits 9 km aerially from the municipal limit — rural, gain fully exempt. The other’s sits 7 km out — urban, fully taxable. Same crop, same buyer profile, two kilometres of geometry worth lakhs in tax. The second test: was it actually farmed? Classification decides the tax; CULTIVATION decides whether your claim survives scrutiny. Revenue records carry seasonal cultivation entries — the evidence that agricultural operations actually happened — and Section 54B leans on exactly that record for its two-year farming condition. Land held bare as pure investment is where exemption claims die at assessment. How the gain is computed Sale price minus purchase cost and expenses. Held 24+ months: long-term. The current long-term regime taxes gains at 12.5% without indexation (indexation having been withdrawn for post-July-2024 sales). And Section 50C looms over the price itself: sell below the stamp-duty value and the department can treat THAT value as your deemed sale price, subject to a tolerance margin — the guideline value quietly setting your tax floor. Rural vs urban at a glance Aspect Rural agricultural land Urban agricultural land Capital asset? No — s.2(14)(iii) excludes it Yes Capital gains tax None LTCG/STCG as applicable TDS on sale (194-IA) Expressly excluded 1% at ₹50 lakh+ (resident seller) Exemption routes Not needed 54B (farmland), 54EC (bonds) The exits: 54B and 54EC Section 54B — individuals and HUFs: reinvest the gain in NEW agricultural land within two years, provided the sold land was farmed for the two years before sale; money not yet reinvested by the return-filing date parks in a Capital Gains Account Scheme; the new land locks in for three years — sell early and the exemption unwinds. Section 54EC — the alternative for long-term gains: NHAI/REC/PFC/IRFC bonds within six months (₹50 lakh cap, five-year lock). The taxes that ride alongside TDS: buyers deduct 1% under 194-IA on urban agricultural land at ₹50 lakh+ — rural land is expressly outside the section. NRI sellers: Section 195 instead, at much higher rates — plan with a lower-deduction certificate. 50C: as above, the stamp-value floor. Quick answers (FAQ) Is rural agricultural land exempt? Fully — it is not a capital asset. How is “rural” defined? The census-population + aerial-distance test above. Indexation still available? Not under the current 12.5% regime. Urban land exemptions? 54B with the farming and lock-in conditions; 54EC bonds. TDS on farmland? Urban yes (₹50L+), rural no. Don’t want to buy farmland again? 54EC bonds, or pay the 12.5% and stay liquid. Bottom line Before selling any farmland, establish three things in writing: the aerial distance to the nearest 10,000+ municipality, the census figure that sets the band, and the cultivation record. Those three lines decide whether the tax is zero, exempt-with-conditions, or fully payable — get a CA’s letter where kilometres decide lakhs. For you: For your JD landowner partners this is THE conversation: many Ranga Reddy parcels sit inside Hyderabad’s 8 km band — urban, taxable — while one village further out is exempt. Knowing which side of the line a family’s land falls (and flagging 54B’s two-year farming condition early) makes you the developer who saved them lakhs before the deal even signed. 2026-11-02|ls-mutation: Mutation of land records: what it is and why it matters Land School · source: “Mutation of Land Records: What It Is and Why It Matters” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Mutation updates the owner’s name in the government’s revenue register after sale, inheritance, gift or partition — it does NOT transfer ownership; registration did that. Skipping it is a top reason buyers fight tax notices and loan rejections years after a purchase. The name changes by state — dakhil kharij, intiqal, patta transfer, khata transfer — the process is the same. A DISPUTED claim cannot be mutated by a revenue officer: it goes to civil court first. The Supreme Court’s position cuts both ways: mutation is not proof of title — but its ABSENCE is proof something was never finished. What mutation is The update of the government’s revenue register to show the CURRENT owner’s name after a sale, inheritance, gift or partition. It is different from the sale deed and registration: mutation affects the tax and revenue record and does not by itself prove legal title. Rural land mutates at the revenue office; urban property at the municipal corporation. The application typically needs the sale deed, previous mutation records and identity proof — and it matters for paying property tax under the right name, and for every future loan or resale. Definition — Mutation (dakhil kharij / khata transfer / patta transfer): the state updating its own ledger of who holds the land — the bridge between the registered deed and the revenue record. Registration changes OWNERSHIP; mutation changes the government’s BOOKS. What the process verifies Not a rubber stamp. The reviewing officer checks that the applicant is the rightful new owner based on a valid transfer document — sale deed, gift deed, or inheritance record — and cross-checks the property’s survey number, area and boundaries against the existing revenue record. What the exercise CANNOT do: establish or guarantee title. It aligns the ledger; it does not adjudicate ownership — which is why a disputed claim goes to civil court, not the Tehsildar. Documents by route How the land came to you Core document for mutation Purchase Registered sale deed Gift Registered gift deed Inheritance (no will) Death certificate + legal-heir certificate Inheritance (will) Death certificate + will (probate where applicable) Partition Registered partition deed / decree Most state portals also want the latest tax receipt and identity proof, whatever the route. One heir applying while others exist? Expect to produce their no-objection letters and an indemnity bond. Why it matters An unmutated register keeps showing the OLD owner though the sale is legally complete. Consequences compound: tax bills keep going to the previous owner while unpaid dues attach to the LAND, not the person; banks reject loans because mutation status is a basic ownership check; resale gets harder because the next buyer’s advocate flags the mismatch instantly; and heir disputes drag for years while land sits under a deceased owner’s name. Example: A buyer purchases in 2018, never mutates. In 2024 a tax-arrears notice arrives — the previous owner’s unpaid dues, now attached to the land. Then the bank declines a mortgage: “record shows a different owner”. Two problems, one skipped application that would have taken a few weeks in 2018. When to apply Immediately after any transaction — some states now run online or even automated mutation for straightforward transfers, others still take manual applications at the revenue office. The two classic delays: assuming the sale deed alone is enough, and inherited land sitting unmutated across a generation. Buying land that moved informally within a family? Ask whether mutation was completed at EACH step, not just the latest. Buying? Check mutation status first The seller-vs-record match is precisely the check that fails on an unmutated parcel — and it is checkable from outside (Dharani in Telangana shows the current pattadar). A mismatch does not always mean fraud; it always means an unfinished step someone must complete before your money moves. Quick answers (FAQ) Does mutation transfer ownership? No — registration does; mutation records it. How long does it take? Weeks for clean files; longer with objections. Can I sell unmutated land? Legally the registered owner can — practically, buyers and their banks balk; mutate first. Heir dispute during mutation? The revenue officer steps aside; civil court decides. Need a lawyer? Not for a clean application; yes the moment there is an objection. Mandatory for agricultural land? Effectively yes — the revenue record drives everything from tax to crop entries. Does it affect loans? Directly — lenders treat it as a gating check. Bottom line Easy to postpone, expensive to ignore. Mutation keeps your name accurate in the records that decide your tax bill, your loan eligibility and your next sale — apply promptly, and when buying, treat the seller’s mutation status as part of the title check. For you: Build it into your buyer experience: hand every plot purchaser a mutation-application pack at registration (or file it for them). Ventures whose buyers’ records are clean resell faster — and resales are your best advertising. On the acquisition side: an unmutated seller is a seller who cannot close on your timeline; surface it in week one, not at the SRO. Glossary — every term, simply HMWSSB — Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply & Sewerage Board, the city’s water utility. Think of it as the single company that both pipes drinking water into your home and pipes sewage away from it. Hyderabad has dozens of STPs along the Musi river and elsewhere, with total installed capacity reported in the thousand-plus MLD range. MLD / MGD — Million Litres per Day and Million Gallons per Day, the two units Indian water utilities use for large volumes; one MGD is roughly 4.55 MLD. Non-potable water — water that is not safe or certified for drinking, but is perfectly fine for uses like curing concrete, dust suppression, watering gardens or flushing — the entire category this scheme targets. Treated wastewater reuse — taking sewage that has already been cleaned at an STP and using it again for a non-drinking purpose, instead of releasing it into a river/lake or letting it go to waste. A simple example: instead of pumping fresh borewell water onto a construction site to settle dust, a tanker brings STP-treated water instead. El Niño — a recurring Pacific Ocean warming pattern that, in India, is often associated with weaker monsoon rainfall. This year’s El Niño-linked rainfall deficit is the stated trigger for Telangana’s whole drought-response programme, this scheme included. NGT (National Green Tribunal) — a specialised Indian court that only hears environmental cases, with the power to set binding standards (like treated-water reuse quality) and order clean-up or compensation. Green Water Tanker / ‘Dial-a-Green Tanker’ — the branded name for this scheme’s delivery fleet; tankers carrying treated wastewater, distinguished from HMWSSB’s ordinary drinking-water tankers by special branding and (reportedly) GPS tracking. Command Control Centre — HMWSSB’s central monitoring room, intended to track tanker bookings, GPS locations and deliveries for this scheme in real time, the way a cab-aggregator tracks its fleet. Tariff — the price per unit of water a bulk user (like a builder) would pay; for this scheme, still unpublished as of today’s search, which is the single biggest open question for anyone trying to budget against it. Bulk user — a water-utility term for a large-volume consumer (a builder, factory or big housing complex) as opposed to an individual household, usually billed on a different tariff structure. CREDAI / NAREDCO — Confederation of Real Estate Developers’ Associations of India / National Real Estate Development Council, the two largest national industry bodies representing property developers, both with active Telangana chapters. The deeper force behind all of this is simple hydrology meeting city growth: Hyderabad’s drinking-water reservoirs (Singur, Manjira, and the Krishna/Godavari-linked schemes) were sized for an earlier, smaller city, and a construction boom plus a weak monsoon year puts the two main demand sources — households and building sites — into direct competition for the same shrinking supply. The water board’s structural answer, visible across 2025–26, has been to build a second, parallel supply chain out of a resource the city used to simply discard: its own sewage. Sharper expert read: a launch date being met while the tariff, final volume target and legal mandate for private builders all remain unpublished is itself the story — the real signal is how long that gap stays open, not the flag-off ceremony. 6. 2026-11-03|ls-scams: Common land scams in India and how to protect yourself Land School · source: “Common Land Scams in India and How to Protect Yourself” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Fraud thrives where records are scattered: ~95% of RoRs are computerised, but only ~68% of cadastral maps. The deadliest scam is the LEGAL-LOOKING one: registered deeds on assigned land are void — registration proves nothing. Seven patterns cover most of the market: forged titles, restricted land, duplicate sales, PoA abuse, encroachment, benami, fake pre-launch schemes. The defence is always the same: pull the records YOURSELF — RoR, EC, prohibited list, title chain. Remote buyers and absentee owners are the favourite targets. Why India’s land market attracts so much fraud Fraud grows wherever information is scarce and checking is hard. India’s records are digitising UNEVENLY — about 95% of Records of Rights computerised but only 68% of cadastral maps, with some districts still on ageing paper — and every state runs its own system. The favourite victims: buyers unfamiliar with local revenue records, people purchasing remotely, and plots whose owners are absent or unaware something is being sold in their name. The most devastating one: restricted land sold as normal Certain land legally CANNOT be freely sold: government-assigned land, tribal land, ceiling-surplus land, endowment (temple) land, forest land. The scam: a legitimate-looking registered document, payment made, registration completed — and years or decades later the government reclaims the land because it was assigned all along. Buyer loses land, money and everything built on it. The legal trap: the prohibited-list mechanism (Section 22-A) only BLOCKS registration of parcels actually on the Collector’s list — unlisted assigned parcels register fine — but the transfer-ban law voids the sale regardless of what any registrar accepted. So: check the prohibited register AND the revenue record’s remarks, always. Seven scams to know 1) Title fraud and forged documents — the most widespread: a fraudster forges papers, poses as owner or PoA holder, sells land that is not theirs; forged paper carries zero legal weight, which is why the CHAIN matters more than the current deed. 2) Restricted-land sales — as above. 3) Duplicate sales — one plot sold to two or more buyers, exploiting slow registration; not a pure first-to-register race (a deed relates back to its execution date under Section 47), but the genuinely prior sale usually prevails and everyone else litigates. 4) PoA abuse — forged, expired or revoked PoAs used to sell without the owner’s knowledge; an unregistered PoA, or one not clearly authorising sale, is a warning. 5) Encroachment folded in — the boundary shown quietly includes government or neighbouring land; good title to part, nothing on the rest; a boundary survey catches it. 6) Benami deals — property in someone else’s name to hide the real buyer; illegal under the 2016 Benami law, with confiscation and up to seven years’ rigorous imprisonment. 7) Fake pre-launch schemes — units sold in unapproved projects with assured-return promises backed by post-dated cheques that bounce; RERA bars selling before registration, so a pre-launch pitch WITHOUT a RERA number is the tell. Definition — Benami transaction: a purchase held in a name-lender’s name while someone else pays and controls it. Since the 2016 amendment the property can be confiscated outright — buyer-side participation is itself the crime. Red flags and what they mean Warning sign What it usually means What to do Price well below market Defect the seller knows and you don’t Slow down; the discount IS the disclosure Pressure to close fast Verification window being shortened deliberately Never pay before checks complete Seller supplies all documents, resists your own EC pull Papers may be curated or forged Pull EC and RoR yourself from official sources Sale via PoA, owner unreachable Possible PoA abuse or a dead/unaware principal Meet or video-verify the owner; check PoA registration “Registration will fix everything” Confusing registration with valid title Remember: void transfers register too No RERA number on a project pitch Unapproved / pre-launch scheme Verify on the state RERA portal before any token Documents to check before any purchase ☐ Title + sale deed — seller’s name matches the record; chain traced 30 years. ☐ Record of Rights — owner, classification, mutation history, restriction remarks. ☐ EC — pulled by YOU from the sub-registrar; never the seller’s copy. ☐ Land use / conversion — classification confirmed; conversion completed if it was agricultural. ☐ Mutation — updated, no restriction notes. ☐ Tax receipts — dues attach to the LAND, not the old owner. ☐ RERA — verified on the portal for any plotted or builder project. ☐ PoA, if involved — authorises sale, registered where required, traceable to the real owner. What maps can and cannot catch Survey-number maps, master-plan overlays and satellite imagery catch boundary and zoning mismatches — whether the parcel’s ground reality matches the deed, and whether it sits in a restricted zone — before a site visit. They cannot read a title chain, tell a forged deed from a genuine one, or check the prohibited list. That work stays with the sub-registrar’s records and a revenue-law advocate. Quick answers (FAQ) Most common scam? Title fraud with forged documents. How do I know if land has transfer restrictions? RoR remarks + the state’s prohibited-property register. Can I buy through a PoA? Yes, with independent verification of the PoA and the principal — PoA sales are not inherently illegitimate. What if I unknowingly bought restricted land? The transfer is void; get a revenue advocate immediately. Is RERA-registered land always safe? Safer — but RERA checks the project, not the title chain; do both. How to report fraud? Police complaint (EOW for large frauds) + civil suit; registration of a case does not undo the transfer, so prevention is the real remedy. Bottom line Nearly every land scam succeeds at the same moment: when the buyer accepts someone else’s paperwork instead of pulling their own. RoR, EC, prohibited list, 30-year chain, boundary survey — five self-service checks defeat all seven scams. For you: Your buyers fear exactly this list — which makes it your marketing. A venture that publishes its own verification file (chain, EC, prohibited-list clearance, DTCP approval) sells trust the unorganised market cannot. Internally: rule — no landowner conversation advances until the RoR and prohibited-list check are done, however warm the introduction. It does NOT certify title. WHICH authority approves depends on where the plot sits — metropolitan areas have their own authorities; DTCP covers the rest. The verification is the LP NUMBER, searched by you on the official portal. A brochure claim is not evidence. A FILE number is not an LP number — “approval in process” means unapproved today. Roads and OSR land inside an approved layout belong to the local body and cannot be sold as plots. What DTCP approval actually certifies A layout permit issued by the Directorate of Town and Country Planning under the state’s town-planning law, confirming the layout meets planning and development standards: road widths, zoning compliance, open spaces, infrastructure provisions. What it never touches: who OWNS the land. An approved layout on a disputed title is still a disputed title with nice roads. Definition — OSR (Open Space Reservation): the share of a layout — typically around 10% — that must be set aside for parks and public purposes and vested in the local body. It is the community’s land; a developer selling “plots” carved from it is selling what is not theirs. DTCP does not apply everywhere The commonest error is checking the right number against the WRONG authority. DTCP’s writ covers the state MINUS the metropolitan planning areas — in Chennai that belt belongs to CMDA; in Hyderabad, HMDA approves inside its boundary while DTCP covers the districts beyond, alongside local and new-town planning authorities issuing equally valid approvals under the same law. First question for any plot: WHOSE jurisdiction is this survey number in? How to verify using the LP number Ask the seller for the approval PROCEEDINGS ORDER and the LP number with its year. Then search it YOURSELF: Telangana — dtcp.telangana.gov.in or the DPMS district-wise approved-layout lists (HMDA’s portal for its belt); Tamil Nadu — onlineppa.tn.gov.in or tcp.tn.gov.in. Older records (roughly ten years plus) often move from the regional office to central storage — an RTI or counter application becomes the route. Then MATCH: survey numbers on the portal against the sale deed; road widths, plot numbers and OSR positions on the approved plan against what is being shown on-site. The plan on the portal is the contract; the site should be its photocopy. Which authority approves what Where the plot sits Approving authority Where to search Metropolitan planning area (e.g. HMDA belt / CMDA) The metropolitan authority Its own approved-layout portal Rest of the state DTCP State DTCP portal / DPMS lists Notified local planning areas Local / new-town planning authority That authority’s records Gram panchayat areas Still the competent planning authority Panchayat “sanction” alone is NOT layout approval The traps that cost buyers money “Approval is in process” — the layout is unapproved TODAY; the number offered is usually a file/application number, and a file number returns nothing on the portal. Gram-panchayat sanction dressed as approval — a panchayat has no power to approve a layout; this is the single most documented fraud pattern in plot sales. OSR and road land sold as plots — reserved areas belong to the local body; corner plots adjoining a reserved zone are where the boundary gets blurred. “Regularisation applied for” — applying under regularisation rules does not make a layout approved; wait for the FINAL order. Approved layout on unconverted land — layout approval and agricultural-land conversion are separate; confirm the conversion order separately. Example: A ₹28-lakh “DTCP-approved” plot near Shadnagar: the brochure prints “LP No. — applied” and a gram-panchayat resolution. Portal search: nothing. Two years later the regularisation application is rejected, the layout stays unapproved, banks refuse loans against every plot in it, and resale prices halve. The five-minute portal search was the whole due diligence. Your checklist before you pay ☐ Confirm which planning authority governs the location. ☐ Get the approval proceedings order + LP number with year. ☐ Search the LP number YOURSELF on the portal; keep the printout. ☐ Match survey numbers, road widths, OSR positions against deed and site. ☐ Treat “in process” and “regularisation applied” as UNAPPROVED. ☐ Run title chain, patta and EC checks separately — approval is not ownership. Quick answers (FAQ) Is approval mandatory before buying? For a safe, financeable, resalable plot — effectively yes. Home loan without it? Banks generally refuse plots in unapproved layouts. Does approval mean clear title? No — planning compliance only. If I buy unapproved anyway? Loan rejection, registration obstacles in some states, regularisation charges if a window opens, demolition exposure if it never does — and a permanent discount at resale. Bottom line One number, one portal, five minutes, your own eyes: the LP-number search is the highest-value check in plot buying. Everything a brochure claims is marketing until the portal agrees. For you: This is YOUR licence to operate — your ventures’ LP numbers are the moat that separates you from the unapproved-layout market. Print the LP number and approved plan into every marketing piece and teach buyers to verify it themselves: the developer who INVITES verification wins the trust war at zero cost. Definition — Field Measurement Book (FMB): the survey department’s measurement sketch of a single survey number — sides, angles, extent. In a boundary fight it is the closest thing to ground truth on paper. The resolution playbook, step by step 1) Assemble your papers — sale deed, mutation entries, tax receipts, old photographs; download the RoR from the state portal; and FIRST check that the survey number on your deed matches the Record of Rights — a mismatch there gets fixed before anything else. 2) Apply for an official government survey — a certified surveyor measures and marks the actual boundary on site; the report becomes central evidence in any later proceeding. 3) Talk first — holding a government survey report changes the conversation from your word against theirs to a neutral document; direct dialogue and state mediation services resolve more than people expect. 4) Legal notice — if the survey supports you, a notice puts your position on record and signals escalation. 5) Revenue authority or civil court — a permanent injunction (Specific Relief Act, s.38) stops ongoing encroachment; a declaratory suit (s.34) establishes ownership and fixes the line; a possession suit recovers taken land. Courts often appoint a local commissioner (CPC Order XXVI Rule 9) to measure and report — influential, though weighed with all the other evidence. Resolution routes compared Route Needs Produces Time Official survey + negotiation Survey fee, both parties talking Marked boundary, often a settlement Weeks–months Mediation Willingness; state mediation services Recorded compromise Months Revenue proceedings Survey report, revenue records Administrative demarcation orders Months Civil suit (injunction / declaration / possession) Advocate, full evidence, court fees Binding decree; commissioner’s measurement Years What digitisation has (and has not) changed Less than the headlines suggest. About 95% of RoRs are computerised — the TEXT record is usually a download. But cadastral maps sit at ~68%, geo-referencing at ~49%, only 11 states/UTs have finished map digitisation, and ULPIN covers a bit over 30% of parcels. Meaning: the record that MATTERS in a boundary fight — the map — is precisely the one most likely to still need verification at the local revenue office. Cross-check every digital map against the official survey record before relying on it. The clock you cannot ignore Twelve years of open, hostile, continuous possession can EXTINGUISH your title through adverse possession — and a suit for possession based on title carries the same twelve-year limitation. An encroachment tolerated politely for a decade is quietly becoming the neighbour’s land. Acting early is not aggression; it is how the limitation law forces you to behave. Example: A family “adjusts” with a neighbour’s shed two metres over the line for fifteen years, then sells — and the buyer’s survey triggers the fight. By then the neighbour’s adverse-possession clock has already run. The survey that cost a few thousand rupees in year one would have settled it while it was still a shed, not a claim. What to do (and avoid) during a dispute DO: pull RoR and cadastral map, confirm deed-vs-record survey number, file for the official survey at the Tehsildar’s office, negotiate with the report in hand, then notice, then court — asking for a commissioner when you get there. AVOID: self-help demolition or fence-moving (it converts your civil case into their criminal complaint), oral settlements with nothing recorded, and waiting out of politeness while the twelve-year clock runs. Quick answers (FAQ) Most reliable evidence? The cadastral map and FMB, plus a fresh official survey. Can maps hold up in court? Yes — weighed with title documents and other evidence. Survey doesn’t match my deed? Fix the record mismatch first; it undermines everything downstream. Can my neighbour claim my land by occupying it? After twelve years of open hostile possession — yes. Check records online? Text records usually; maps often still need the revenue office. Bottom line Boundary fights are won on certified measurements, not memories. Survey early, record everything, act inside the limitation clock — and treat the few-thousand-rupee survey as the cheapest insurance land ownership offers. For you: For a plotting developer boundaries are the product itself — every plot you sell is a promise about a line. Fresh FMB-matched survey BEFORE layout design, stones planted and photographed at handover, and the survey report in each buyer’s file: that ritual is why organised ventures command premiums over the neighbour selling “by the tree line”. 2026-11-05|ls-death-transfer: How to transfer land ownership after the owner’s death Land School · source: “How to Transfer Land Ownership After the Owner’s Death” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Title does not shift automatically at death — the record keeps the dead owner’s name until someone files for mutation. Probate stopped being MANDATORY anywhere in India on 20 December 2025 (Repealing and Amending Act, 2025 removed Section 213) — but banks and buyers still ask for it. Without a will, PERSONAL law decides: Hindu, Muslim and Christian families on the same street follow different rules. A succession certificate covers bank accounts and securities — NOT land. India has no transfer-on-death deed; the nearest equivalent is a registered settlement or gift deed made while the owner is alive. Why ownership does not transfer automatically An heir does not become the recorded owner by grief alone — someone has to FILE, and the filing is mutation: updating the revenue and municipal record so the state knows who now owes land revenue and property tax. The application goes to the concerned revenue authority with the death certificate, proof of heirship, and the existing land records. With a will vs without one With a will: land passes directly to named beneficiaries through the executor — sometimes involving probate. Without a will (intestate): ownership follows the personal succession law of the deceased’s religion — the Hindu Succession Act for Hindus (daughters holding EQUAL coparcenary rights since 2005), Muslim personal law with its fixed shares, the Indian Succession Act for Christians and Parsis. The intestate route usually needs court-issued heirship paperwork, making it slower — which is the practical argument for a will. Definition — Probate: a court’s certification that a will is genuine. Since 20 December 2025 it is mandatory NOWHERE in India — the old Section 213 requirement (which bound certain wills, notably in the presidency towns) was repealed. But the market has memory: banks and cautious buyers still ASK for probate on willed property, so sometimes heirs obtain it for smoothness even though the law no longer compels it. Legal-heir certificate vs succession certificate Constantly confused, differently scoped. A legal-heir certificate establishes WHO the heirs are — used for utility transfers, pensions, bank formalities, and as the heirship proof in land mutation. A succession certificate , issued by a civil court, authorises the holder to collect the deceased’s DEBTS, SECURITIES and MOVABLE assets — it does not itself convey land. For immovable property, courts and offices weigh the succession certificate alongside other documents, but the land transfer runs on heirship proof + mutation (or a court partition where heirs contest). Documents required ☐ Death certificate — first, everything waits on it. ☐ Legal-heir certificate (or the will + executor papers). ☐ The land records — deed, RoR/passbook, tax receipts. ☐ Co-heirs’ written NOCs where one heir applies. ☐ EC — checking for loans or claims riding on the land. ☐ For heirs abroad: a PoA that SPECIFICALLY authorises applying for the heir certificate and mutation — generic property clauses stall at the counter. Why India has no transfer-on-death deed — and the substitute Several countries let owners name a death-beneficiary on the deed itself; India does not. The working equivalent: a registered settlement or gift deed executed while the owner is alive , reserving a LIFE INTEREST — the owner keeps possession until death, and the property vests in the named person automatically afterwards. Stamped, registered, and it takes effect without anyone approaching a court later. For families who know exactly where land should go, it converts a future dispute into a present document. The steps, in order 1) Death certificate. 2) Establish heirship — get the legal-heir certificate proactively, not when an office finally asks. 3) Co-heirs’ NOCs in writing BEFORE filing — one heir applying alone invites an objection. 4) Pull the EC and revenue record — surface any loan or claim now. 5) File mutation with the revenue authority. 6) Only then list, sell, or borrow. Example: Three siblings inherit; the eldest files mutation alone “to keep it simple”. A sister objects, the revenue officer freezes the entry, and the file crosses into civil-court territory — two years gone. The written NOCs would have cost a week. Selling inherited land Most inherited land eventually reaches the market — and that is where unfinished mutation surfaces, because any buyer’s verification matches seller against record, and the record still names the deceased. Heirs who complete mutation BEFORE listing sell on their own timeline; those who do not discover the gap at the sub-registrar, in front of their buyer. Quick answers (FAQ) Does ownership pass automatically to heirs? By succession law, beneficially yes — but the RECORD moves only on filing. Is probate mandatory? No, since 20 Dec 2025 — though lenders and buyers may still request it. No will? Personal law distributes; heirship certificate + mutation execute. Transfer-on-death deed? Not in India — use a registered settlement/gift deed with life interest. Do daughters have equal rights? Yes — equal coparcenary rights in Hindu law since 2005. How long does it take? Clean, cooperative files: weeks to a few months; contested ones: years. Bottom line Death moves rights; paperwork moves records. Certificate, heirship, NOCs, EC, mutation — done early, in order, it is administration; done late or out of order, it is litigation. For you: Half the parcels you negotiate are inherited — so your first question to any selling family is “is mutation complete in the CURRENT generation’s names?”. If not, your timeline is not theirs to promise. And structurally: an incomplete heir set signing your agreement is a future injunction on your layout — collect every heir’s signature or a court partition first.
